Pour-over is a manual brewing method that lets you control the process for a clean, flavorful cup. It highlights the unique notes in your beans better than many automatic machines. The technique uses a simple dripper, filter, and hot water poured over grounds in stages.

Start with fresh beans. Buy whole beans roasted within the past two to four weeks for peak flavor. Older beans lose aroma and taste flat. Single-origin coffees from places like Ethiopia or Colombia often shine in pour-over because their bright, fruity, or floral notes come through clearly.

Consider roast level next. Lighter roasts keep more of the bean's original character and acidity. Medium roasts balance sweetness and body. Darker roasts bring chocolate and nutty tones but can mask subtleties. Experiment with a few bags to find what you like.

Store beans properly. Keep them in an airtight container at room temperature away from sunlight and moisture. Avoid the fridge because condensation can harm freshness. Grind only what you need right before brewing to preserve oils and aromas.

If the grind is too fine, water lingers too long and pulls out bitter compounds. The coffee tastes harsh or astringent. If it is too coarse, water rushes through and leaves the grounds under-extracted. The cup ends up weak and sour. Adjust your grinder one notch at a time until the brew tastes balanced.

Water temperature plays a big role in dissolving the right flavors. Use water between 195 and 205 degrees Fahrenheit, or about 90 to 96 degrees Celsius.
